explain.title: What chemistry studies
explain.body: Chemistry studies substances: their properties, composition and structure. It also studies physical and chemical changes in matter and the laws or principles governing those changes. Composition means which elements and compounds are present and their percentages; structure means how atoms are arranged.

explain.title: Why chemistry has branches
explain.body: Chemistry is a widely spread, complex subject. Dividing it into branches allows scientists to focus on specific aspects and work towards breakthroughs and advancements.

explain.title: Recognise branches by their focus
explain.body: Physical chemistry studies behaviour at atomic and molecular levels. Analytical chemistry analyses substances and their components. Biochemistry studies chemical substances and vital processes in living organisms. Nuclear chemistry studies reactions in the nucleus.

explain.title: More branch clues
explain.body: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, with certain simple carbon salts excluded. Inorganic chemistry studies elements and compounds containing little or no carbon. Environmental chemistry studies chemical phenomena in the planet; medicinal chemistry deals with medicines; polymer chemistry with polymers; geochemistry with Earth’s chemical composition; and astrochemistry with molecules and ions in space.

mistakes: Do not confuse analytical chemistry, which analyses components and concentrations, with physical chemistry, which studies behaviour and physical laws.
Do not say organic chemistry studies every carbon-containing substance: the textbook excludes simple salts such as carbonates, bicarbonates, oxides and carbides.
Do not confuse biochemistry with organic chemistry: biochemistry focuses on chemical substances and processes in living organisms.
Do not choose nuclear chemistry for reactions involving electrons outside the nucleus; nuclear chemistry concerns reactions and transformations in the nucleus.

explain.title: Matter and its states
explain.body: Anything other than energy which carries weight and occupies volume is called matter. A state of matter is one of the many distinct forms in which matter can exist. The three primary states are solid, liquid and gas; plasma is also observed in everyday life.

explain.title: Solids, liquids and gases
explain.body: Gas molecules are very widely apart, have no order and experience very weak intermolecular forces. Liquid molecules are closely attached but move randomly, with significant intermolecular forces. Solid particles are closely packed, strongly attracted and fixed at their positions, where they can oscillate about their mean positions.

explain.title: Plasma and intermediate states
explain.body: Plasma is composed of particles with very high kinetic energy and can be considered a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions and photons. Supercritical fluids are highly compressed states showing properties of gases and liquids. Liquid crystals have properties between conventional liquids and crystalline solids.

explain.title: Graphene and exotic states
explain.body: Graphene is a two-dimensional crystal consisting of a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern. States of matter not commonly encountered are called exotic states of matter.

mistakes: Do not say that gas molecules are close together; they are very widely apart.
Do not say that solid particles travel freely; they remain fixed at their positions and oscillate about their mean positions.
Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas: the section describes plasma as a partially ionized gas.
Do not confuse a supercritical fluid with a liquid crystal: the former shows properties of gases and liquids, while the latter has properties between conventional liquids and crystalline solids.
When comparing graphite and graphene, do not omit the key difference: graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms.

yourTurn.question: Q1.2. What are allotropic forms? Explain the allotropic forms of carbon and sulphur. How does coal differ from diamond?
solution: Allotropic forms are different structural forms of the same element that can have quite different physical and chemical properties.
Carbon exists in three main allotropic forms: diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene (C₆₀).
Diamond has a giant macromolecular structure, while graphite has a layered structure of hexagonal rings of carbon.
Buckminster fullerene (C₆₀) consists of a cage-like sphere made of carbon atoms arranged in pentagons and hexagons.
Sulphur exists in two crystalline allotropic forms: rhombic and monoclinic; rhombic sulphur is more stable.
Coal is an amorphous, impure form of carbon, whereas diamond is a crystalline form of carbon.
yourTurn.answer: Carbon has diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene forms; sulphur has rhombic and monoclinic forms, with rhombic more stable. Coal is amorphous and impure, while diamond is crystalline.

explain.title: What allotropy means

explain.title: Carbon has different structures

explain.title: Sulphur has two crystalline forms

explain.title: Remember the fullerene facts

explain.title: Elements
explain.body: An element is the simplest form of matter. It is a pure substance containing the same kind of atoms. It cannot be broken down into simpler particles by ordinary chemical reactions. When an element exists in the form of atoms, it is represented by a symbol, such as Na for sodium and Ca for calcium.

explain.title: Compounds
explain.body: A compound is a pure substance. It is formed by the chemical combination of two or more atoms of different elements. These atoms combine in a fixed ratio by weight. A compound can be broken into its constituent elements by a chemical reaction, and its properties differ from those of the elements forming it.

explain.title: Mixtures
explain.body: Mixture is an impure compound. A sample of matter having more than one type of elements or compounds mixed together in any ratio, is called a mixture. Its components retain their identities and specific properties, are not chemically bound together, and can be separated by physical methods.

explain.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures
explain.body: A mixture may be homogeneous or heterogeneous. A solution of common salt in water is homogeneous, while a sample of rock is heterogeneous. The properties of a mixture are the sum of those of its components.

mistakes: Do not say that the components of a mixture are chemically combined; they are not chemically bound and can be separated by physical methods.

explain.title: True solution
explain.body: A solution is such a mixture in which solute particles are completely homogenized in the solvent e.g. dissolution of sodium chloride or copper sulphate in water. The solute particles in such a solution cannot be seen by the naked eye. If solution is filtered, these particles pass through the pores of filter paper leaving no residue. Such a solution is called a true solution.

explain.title: Suspension
explain.body: A suspension, on the other hand, is a mixture in which solute particles do not dissolve in the solvent. We can actually see these particles. If a suspension is kept for some time, these particles settle down. Again, if this suspension is filtered, the particles in it cannot pass through the pores of filter paper and can be collected as a residue. A mixture of chalk in water is an example of suspension.

explain.title: Colloidal solution
explain.body: Besides a true solution and a suspension, there is a third form of solution called colloidal solution. In this type, the solute particles do not homogenize with solvent. These particles are a little bit bigger than the solute particles present in the true solution but not big enough to be seen with a naked eye like the particles present in a suspension. If kept for some time, the particles of a colloidal solution do not settle down. On filtration, these particles pass through the filter paper like the particles of a true solution. Starch solution and white of an egg are the common examples of colloidal solutions.

explain.title: A quick way to compare them
explain.body: True-solution particles cannot be seen and pass through filter paper. Colloidal particles are also not visible to the naked eye, do not settle, and pass through filter paper. Suspension particles are visible, settle down, and are collected as residue during filtration.

mistakes: Do not say that colloidal particles settle down; the textbook says they do not.
Do not say that colloidal particles are trapped by ordinary filter paper; they pass through it.
Do not confuse visibility with filtration: both true-solution and colloidal particles pass through filter paper, but suspension particles do not.
Do not call chalk mixed with water a true solution; it is a suspension.

explain.title: Chemistry has different branches
explain.body: Chemistry covers many substances, reactions, and applications. Branches make this large subject easier to organize and allow detailed study. For example, biochemistry deals with chemical processes in living things, while analytical chemistry identifies substances and measures their amounts.

explain.title: Matter has several states
explain.body: Solids, liquids, and gases are familiar states. Plasma is an ionized gas, liquid crystals have properties between liquids and crystalline solids, and supercritical fluids form above a substance's critical temperature and pressure.

explain.title: Structure affects properties
explain.body: Carbon forms different allotropes. Graphite contains layers that slide over one another, so it is slippery; graphene is a single layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal pattern. Sulphur also has different forms, including rhombic and monoclinic sulphur.

explain.title: Solutions and solubility
explain.body: A solute dissolves in a solvent to form a solution. Different solutes have different solubilities because they interact differently with the solvent. For most solids, solubility increases as temperature rises; gases dissolved in liquids generally become less soluble as temperature rises.

explain.title: Crystallization purifies a substance
explain.body: Dissolve a soluble solid in hot water, remove insoluble impurities by filtration, and cool the clear solution. As solubility falls, crystals form. Collect and dry the crystals; many soluble impurities stay in the remaining solution.

mistakes: Do not confuse plasma with an ordinary gas: plasma contains charged particles because the gas has been ionized.
Do not describe graphene as many layers; graphene is one layer, while graphite has many layers.
Do not confuse analytical chemistry, which identifies and measures substances, with physical chemistry, which studies properties and reaction rates.
When explaining dissolution, include both the separation of ions and their interaction with water molecules.
Do not say that all solubilities change in the same direction with temperature; most solid solutes and gases behave differently.
For crystallization, do not cool the solution before removing insoluble impurities, and do not forget to collect and dry the crystals.
Do not call coal a pure crystalline form of carbon; distinguish it from diamond.

notes.title: Chemistry and its branches
notes.answer: Chemistry studies the properties, composition and structure of substances, their changes, and the principles governing those changes.
notes.explanation: Chemistry studies substances: what they are made of, how their atoms are arranged, what properties they have, and how they change. Its branches let scientists focus on particular kinds of substances or questions.
notes.simple: Chemistry is the study of substances and how they behave or change.
examples: Finding the concentration of a substance in a sample is studied in analytical chemistry.
Studying reactions in an atom’s nucleus is studied in nuclear chemistry.
steps: Identify the main subject of the question, such as composition, reaction rate, or a living process.
Match that subject to the branch that studies it.
For a reaction in an atom’s nucleus, choose nuclear chemistry.

notes.title: States of Matter
notes.answer: Plasma is a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions and photons.
notes.explanation: Matter occurs in different states. The arrangement, spacing and movement of particles, and the strength of the forces between them, help explain how solids, liquids and gases differ.
notes.simple: Matter is the material around us. Its particles can be arranged and move in different ways, giving matter different states.
examples: A gas has particles far apart and is easily compressed.
A solid has particles closely packed in fixed positions and has a definite shape.
steps: Identify the state being described.
Recall its particle arrangement and movement.
Connect those particle features to the state’s properties.
notes.checkAnswer: Plasma is a partially ionized gas containing electrons, ions and photons.

notes.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
notes.answer: A mixture is formed when more than one type of element or compound is mixed together in any ratio.
notes.explanation: Most everyday materials are mixtures: they contain more than one element or compound mixed together. A mixture can have a uniform composition, like salt water, or a non-uniform composition, like rock.
notes.simple: An element has one kind of atom. A compound has different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio. A mixture has substances mixed together in any ratio.
examples: Salt water is a homogeneous mixture because its concentration is uniform throughout.
Rock is a heterogeneous mixture because its constituents are not distributed uniformly.
steps: Check whether the sample contains one kind of atom, different elements chemically combined, or substances mixed together.
If substances are mixed, check whether the composition is uniform throughout or varies from place to place.
Name it as an element, compound, homogeneous mixture or heterogeneous mixture.

notes.title: Allotropic forms
notes.answer: Allotropic forms are different structural forms of the same element that can have quite different physical and chemical properties.
notes.explanation: Allotropy means that the same element can exist in different structural forms, and those forms can have different physical and chemical properties. Carbon has forms such as diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene; sulphur has rhombic and monoclinic forms.
notes.simple: One element can have different forms because its atoms can be arranged differently. These forms may have different properties.
examples: Carbon: diamond, graphite and Buckminster fullerene (C₆₀).
Sulphur: rhombic and monoclinic sulphur; rhombic sulphur is more stable.
steps: Identify the element.
Name its different structural forms.
State a property or structural feature that distinguishes the forms.

notes.title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
notes.answer: A mixture is a sample of matter containing more than one type of element or compound mixed together in any ratio.
notes.explanation: Elements, compounds and mixtures differ in how their particles are made and joined. Elements contain one kind of atom; compounds contain elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; mixtures contain substances mixed without chemical bonding.
notes.simple: An element has one kind of atom. A compound has different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio. A mixture has different substances together but not chemically joined.
examples: Water (H₂O) is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Salt water is a mixture: salt and water are mixed, and the salt retains its identity.
steps: Check whether the sample contains one kind of atom, chemically combined elements, or mixed substances.
For a compound, look for chemical combination in a fixed ratio.
For a mixture, remember that its components retain their properties and can be separated physically.

notes.title: Distinguishing solutions, colloids and suspensions
notes.answer: True solutions and colloids pass through filter paper; suspension particles are trapped as residue.
notes.explanation: A true solution has particles too small to see; they pass through filter paper and do not leave residue. Colloidal particles also pass through filter paper and do not settle, but they are larger than true-solution particles. Suspension particles can be seen, settle on standing, and are trapped by filter paper.
notes.simple: Check whether particles can be seen, settle down, or stay behind when the mixture is filtered.
examples: Salt dissolved in water is a true solution.
Starch solution is a colloidal solution; chalk mixed with water is a suspension.

notes.answer: The extra sugar does not dissolve and settles at the bottom.

notes.title: How temperature affects solubility
notes.answer: Temperature usually increases the solubility of solids, but the effect varies by substance; gas solubility usually decreases as temperature increases.
notes.explanation: Solubility tells us how much solute can dissolve in a fixed amount of solvent at a particular temperature. Heating often increases the solubility of solids, but not always; the effect depends on the substance. Cooling a hot, concentrated solution can make crystals form.
notes.simple: Heating often helps more solid dissolve, while cooling can make some dissolved solid form crystals. This is not true for every substance.
examples: KNO₃ becomes much more soluble in hot water, so it can crystallize when the solution cools.
Gas solubility usually decreases as temperature rises, so cold soda water keeps more carbon dioxide dissolved.

Solutions and crystallization also help explain how substances dissolve and how they can be purified.

This describes the arrangement of gas molecules.
Random movement may describe liquids, but solids are relatively incompressible.
Partial ionization is associated with plasma.

quiz.stem: Which description identifies a liquid crystal?
options: A state whose properties are between those of conventional liquids and crystalline solids.
A highly compressed state that shows properties of gases and liquids.
A partially ionized gas.
A state made of particles fixed in a rigid arrangement.
rationales: This is correct: liquid crystals have properties between conventional liquids and crystalline solids.
This describes a supercritical fluid.
This describes plasma.
This is a description of a solid, not a liquid crystal.

quiz.stem: Which feature of plasma is stated in the section?
options: It is composed of particles with very high kinetic energy.
It has a definite shape and fixed volume.
Its particles are closely attached but move randomly.
It consists of one layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal pattern.
rationales: This is correct: plasma is composed of particles with very high kinetic energy.
A definite shape and fixed volume describe solids.
This describes the movement and spacing of liquid molecules.
This describes graphene.

quiz.stem: Which statement about supercritical fluids is correct?
options: They show both properties of gases and liquids.
They have the fixed shape of crystalline solids.
They consist only of electrons and ions.
They are states seen only in everyday life.
rationales: This is correct: supercritical fluids are highly compressed states showing properties of both gases and liquids.
The section does not describe supercritical fluids as having the fixed shape of solids.
The section describes plasma, not supercritical fluids, as containing ionized particles.
The section gives supercritical fluids as an intermediate state, not an everyday state.

quiz.stem: What are exotic states of matter?
options: States of matter not commonly encountered.
States made only of crystalline solids.
The three primary states of matter.
Materials that do not occupy volume.
rationales: This is correct: states of matter not commonly encountered are called exotic states.
The term is not limited to crystalline solids.
The three primary states are solid, liquid and gas, not exotic states.
Matter occupies volume, so this does not define exotic states.

quiz.stem: Which description identifies graphene?
options: A single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal pattern.
A liquid whose molecules are arranged randomly.
A highly compressed mixture of gas and liquid.
A partially ionized gas found in welding arcs.
rationales: This is correct: graphene is a two-dimensional crystal of one layer of carbon atoms in a hexagonal pattern.
This does not describe graphene; it resembles a description of a liquid.
This describes properties associated with a supercritical fluid.
This describes plasma, not graphene.

quiz.stem: Which description best identifies an element?
options: A pure substance containing only one kind of atom
Two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio
Two or more substances mixed in any ratio
A sample with a composition that varies from place to place
rationales: Correct: the textbook defines an element as a pure substance containing the same kind of atoms.
Incorrect: this describes a compound, not an element.
Incorrect: this describes a mixture.
Incorrect: a composition that varies across a sample is a feature of a heterogeneous mixture.

quiz.stem: Which of these is a compound?
options: Copper wire
Water
Salt water
Rock
rationales: Incorrect: copper is an element.
Correct: water is an example of a compound in the textbook.
Incorrect: salt water is a mixture of salt and water.
Incorrect: rock is a heterogeneous mixture.

quiz.stem: In what ratio may the substances in a mixture be combined?
options: A fixed ratio
Any ratio
A ratio that changes from one part to another
No elements or compounds
rationales: Incorrect: a fixed ratio is characteristic of a compound.
Correct: a mixture forms when substances are combined in any ratio.
Incorrect: variation from place to place may describe a heterogeneous mixture, but it does not define the ratio in which its substances are mixed.
Incorrect: mixtures are made from elements or compounds, or both.

quiz.stem: Which feature identifies a heterogeneous mixture?
options: Its composition is uniform throughout
It contains only one kind of atom
Its constituents are chemically joined in a fixed ratio
Its composition varies in different parts
rationales: Incorrect: uniform composition throughout describes a homogeneous mixture.
Incorrect: one kind of atom describes an element.
Incorrect: chemically joined constituents in a fixed ratio describe a compound.
Correct: a heterogeneous mixture has different concentrations of its constituents in different parts.

quiz.stem: Which of these is shown as a mixture in the textbook's examples?
options: Iron sulphide
Zinc
Chocolate
Water
rationales: Incorrect: iron sulphide is shown as a compound.
Incorrect: zinc is an element.
Correct: chocolate is shown as a mixture.
Incorrect: water is a compound.

quiz.stem: Which description best identifies a compound?
options: A pure substance with the same kind of atoms
A pure substance made of different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio
Elements or compounds mixed in any ratio
A substance whose composition is always non-uniform
rationales: Incorrect: this is the definition of an element.
Correct: a compound is made of different elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
Incorrect: this describes a mixture.
Incorrect: compounds have uniform composition, not necessarily non-uniform composition.

quiz.stem: What makes a salt-water solution homogeneous?
options: It has the same concentration throughout
Its components are different in different parts
It contains only one type of element
Its components are chemically bonded in a fixed ratio
rationales: Correct: the textbook says its concentration is uniform throughout.
Incorrect: different composition in different parts describes a heterogeneous mixture.
Incorrect: salt water contains more than one substance.
Incorrect: fixed-ratio chemical bonding describes a compound, not a solution.

quiz.stem: Which pair consists of the two allotropic forms of oxygen named in your textbook?
options: O₂ and O₃
CO₂ and CO
H₂ and H₂O
N₂ and NH₃
rationales: This is correct because oxygen exists as oxygen (O₂) and ozone (O₃).
This is incorrect because carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide are different compounds, not allotropes of oxygen.
This is incorrect because H₂ and H₂O are different substances, not forms of one element.
This is incorrect because N₂ and NH₃ are different substances and do not represent oxygen allotropes.

quiz.stem: Which one is not a main allotropic form of carbon?
options: Diamond
Graphite
Buckminster fullerene
Monoclinic sulphur
rationales: This is incorrect because diamond is one of the main allotropic forms of carbon.
This is incorrect because graphite is one of the main allotropic forms of carbon.
This is incorrect because Buckminster fullerene is one of the main allotropic forms of carbon.
This is correct because monoclinic sulphur is a form of sulphur, not carbon.

quiz.stem: Which structural description is given for diamond?
options: A giant macromolecular structure
A layered structure of hexagonal rings
A cage of charged molecules
Spheres made of sulphur atoms
rationales: This is correct because the text describes diamond as having a giant macromolecular structure.
This is incorrect because the text gives the layered hexagonal-ring structure for graphite.
This is incorrect because the fullerene molecule is stated to be not charged.
This is incorrect because the text describes Buckminster fullerene as carbon atoms arranged in spheres.

quiz.stem: In Buckminster fullerene (C₆₀), the atoms are arranged in spheres made of which shapes?
options: Pentagons and hexagons
Squares and triangles
Only hexagons
Only pentagons
rationales: This is correct because the text states that the spheres contain atoms arranged in pentagons and hexagons.
This is incorrect because the text does not describe squares and triangles in the fullerene structure.
This is incorrect because the text names both pentagons and hexagons.
This is incorrect because the text names both pentagons and hexagons.

quiz.stem: Which statement about rhombic sulphur agrees with the section?
options: It is more stable than rhombic sulphur.
It is more stable than monoclinic sulphur.
It is the only crystalline form of sulphur.
It is a form of carbon.
rationales: This is incorrect because rhombic sulphur, not monoclinic sulphur, is more stable.
This is correct because the text says rhombic sulphur is more stable than monoclinic sulphur.
This is incorrect because the text names two crystalline forms of sulphur.
This is incorrect because rhombic sulphur is a form of sulphur.

quiz.stem: Which pair of properties does the text give for fullerene C₆₀?
options: It is soft and cannot conduct electricity.
It is hard and conducts electricity.
It is soft and conducts electricity.
It is hard and cannot conduct electricity.
rationales: This is correct because the text says fullerene C₆₀ is soft and cannot conduct electricity.
This is incorrect because neither property matches the text's description of C₆₀.
This is incorrect because the text says C₆₀ cannot conduct electricity.
This is incorrect because the text describes C₆₀ as soft.

quiz.stem: Which carbon form is described as having layers of hexagonal rings?
options: Diamond
Graphite
Buckminster fullerene
Rhombic sulphur
rationales: This is incorrect because diamond is described as having a giant macromolecular structure.
This is correct because graphite has a layered structure of hexagonal rings of carbon.
This is incorrect because Buckminster fullerene has a cage-like spherical structure.
This is incorrect because rhombic sulphur is an allotropic form of sulphur.

quiz.stem: Which statement is not given as a feature of the fullerene structure in the section?
options: The molecule has no boundaries.
The molecule has no unpaired electrons.
The molecule is not charged.
The molecule has a high melting point.
rationales: This is incorrect because the text says the fullerene molecule has no boundaries.
This is incorrect because the text says the fullerene molecule has no unpaired electrons.
This is incorrect because the text says the fullerene molecule is not charged.
This is correct because the text says fullerene C₆₀ has a low melting point, not a high one.

quiz.stem: Which description matches an element?
options: A pure substance containing the same kind of atoms
Different substances chemically combined in any ratio
Two or more substances mixed in a fixed ratio
A pure substance that can always be separated physically
rationales: Correct: an element is a pure substance containing the same kind of atoms.
Incorrect: chemical combination describes a compound, and compounds form in fixed ratios.
Incorrect: substances mixed in any ratio describe a mixture.
Incorrect: an element cannot be broken down by ordinary chemical reactions.

quiz.stem: Which statement is a property of a mixture?
options: Its components retain their identities and properties
Its elements are always present in any ratio
It can be separated only by chemical reactions
Its properties are always different from its components
rationales: Correct: each component of a mixture retains its identity and specific properties.
Incorrect: a mixture may be in any ratio, but this option incorrectly describes its elements as having a fixed identity in that ratio.
Incorrect: mixtures can be separated by physical methods.
Incorrect: this is a property of compounds, not mixtures.

quiz.stem: What distinguishes a compound from a mixture?
options: The atoms of its elements combine in a fixed ratio by weight
Its components can be separated by physical methods
It contains only one kind of atom
Its components always retain their original properties
rationales: Correct: the elements in a compound combine in a fixed ratio by weight.
Incorrect: physical separation is a feature of mixtures.
Incorrect: one kind of atom describes an element.
Incorrect: mixture components retain their properties; compound properties differ from those of its elements.

quiz.stem: Which of these is a compound?
options: Water
Salt dissolved in water
A sample of rock
A mixture of sand and iron filings
rationales: Correct: water is a compound made from hydrogen and oxygen in a fixed ratio.
Incorrect: salt dissolved in water is a mixture.
Incorrect: rock is given as an example of a heterogeneous mixture.
Incorrect: sand and iron filings are mixed, not chemically combined.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes how the components of a mixture are held together?
options: The components are chemically bound together
The components are not chemically bound and can be separated physically
The components must be present in a fixed ratio
The mixture has properties different from all its components
rationales: Incorrect: chemical bonding between elements is characteristic of compounds.
Correct: mixture components are not chemically bound and can be separated by physical methods.
Incorrect: a fixed ratio is a feature of compounds, not mixtures.
Incorrect: the textbook states that mixture properties are the sum of those of its components.

quiz.stem: Which is an example of a homogeneous mixture?
options: A solution of common salt in water
Water
Hydrogen chloride
Ammonia
rationales: Correct: a solution of common salt in water is given as a homogeneous mixture.
Incorrect: water is a compound.
Incorrect: hydrogen chloride is a compound.
Incorrect: ammonia is a compound.

quiz.stem: Which statement about elements is correct?
options: It can be broken into simpler particles by ordinary chemical reactions
It is represented by a symbol when it exists as atoms
It always exists as independent molecules
It is made from different elements in a fixed ratio
rationales: Incorrect: an element cannot be broken down into simpler particles by ordinary chemical reactions.
Correct: an element existing as atoms is represented by a symbol, such as Na or Ca.
Incorrect: some elements exist as atoms, while gaseous elements may exist as molecules and noble gases are monoatomic.
Incorrect: different elements combined in a fixed ratio describe a compound.

quiz.stem: Which statement about compounds is correct?
options: The properties of a compound are always different from those of the elements forming it
A compound's components can always be separated by physical methods
A compound contains only one type of element
A compound has no fixed ratio of its elements
rationales: Correct: the properties of a compound are always different from those of the elements from which it is formed.
Incorrect: a compound is broken into its constituent elements by a chemical reaction.
Incorrect: a compound is formed from two or more atoms of different elements.
Incorrect: the elements in a compound combine in a fixed ratio by weight.

quiz.stem: Which observation is common to both a true solution and a colloidal solution when they are filtered?
options: The particles settle down after standing.
The particles pass through filter paper.
The particles are visible to the naked eye.
The particles can be collected as filter-paper residue.
rationales: Settling is a feature of a suspension, not of a true solution or colloid.
This is correct: both true-solution and colloidal particles pass through filter paper.
True-solution particles and colloidal particles cannot be seen with the naked eye.
Particles collected as residue are characteristic of a suspension.

quiz.stem: Which observation best distinguishes a suspension from a colloidal solution?
options: The particles settle down on standing.
The particles are completely homogenized in the solvent.
The particles pass through filter paper without leaving residue.
The particles cannot be seen with the naked eye.
rationales: This is correct: suspension particles settle down, while colloidal particles do not.
Complete homogenization describes a true solution.
Both colloids and true solutions pass through filter paper.
Suspension particles can be seen with the naked eye.

quiz.stem: A mixture has particles that can be seen, settle when left standing, and are trapped by filter paper. What is it?
options: True solution
Colloidal solution
Suspension
Solvent
rationales: True-solution particles cannot be seen and pass through filter paper.
Colloidal particles do not settle and pass through filter paper.
This is correct: all three observations describe a suspension.
A solvent is the substance in which a solute dissolves, not this type of mixture.

quiz.stem: Which mixture is an example of a suspension?
options: Chalk in water
Starch solution
White of an egg
Copper sulphate dissolved in water
rationales: This is correct: chalk particles do not dissolve and form a suspension in water.
Starch solution is given as a colloidal solution.
White of an egg is given as a colloidal solution.
Copper sulphate dissolved in water forms a true solution.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes the particles in a true solution?
options: They settle down after a short time.
They are trapped by filter paper.
They are too small to be seen with the naked eye.
They pass through filter paper.
rationales: True-solution particles do not settle down on standing.
True-solution particles pass through filter paper instead of being trapped.
This is correct: true-solution particles cannot be seen with the naked eye.
This is true of true-solution particles, but it does not distinguish them from colloidal particles; the question asks for the defining description given in the section.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes the size and visibility of colloidal particles?
options: They settle down on standing.
They are a little bigger than true-solution particles but cannot be seen with the naked eye.
They are completely homogenized in the solvent.
They cannot pass through filter paper.
rationales: The section says colloidal particles do not settle down.
This is correct: colloidal particles are larger than true-solution particles but are not visible to the naked eye.
The section says colloidal particles do not homogenize with the solvent.
Colloidal particles pass through filter paper.

quiz.stem: What happens to colloidal particles when the mixture is left standing and then filtered?
options: They stay suspended forever and cannot be filtered.
They pass through filter paper and do not settle down.
They settle down but pass through filter paper.
They are visible and leave no residue on filtration.
rationales: Colloidal particles pass through filter paper; the section does not say they stay suspended forever.
This is correct: colloidal particles do not settle and pass through filter paper.
Colloidal particles do not settle down.
Colloidal particles are not visible to the naked eye, and they pass through filter paper.

quiz.stem: Which mixture is a true solution rather than a colloid or suspension?
options: Copper sulphate dissolved in water
Chalk mixed with water
Starch solution
White of an egg
rationales: This is correct: copper sulphate dissolved in water is given as an example of a true solution.
Chalk in water is an example of a suspension.
Starch solution is a colloidal solution.
White of an egg is a colloidal solution.

quiz.stem: Which statement describes an unsaturated solution?
options: It can dissolve more solute at that temperature.
It contains no solvent.
Extra solute always settles at the bottom.
It contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve.
rationales: This is correct because an unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at that temperature.
This is wrong because a solution contains a solvent.
This is wrong because extra solute settles when the solution has reached saturation.
This is wrong because the maximum dissolved amount describes a saturated solution.

quiz.stem: What is a saturated solution?
options: It can still dissolve more solute.
It has dissolved the maximum amount of solute at that temperature.
It contains no solute.
It must be a mixture of two liquids.
rationales: This is wrong because a solution that can dissolve more solute is unsaturated.
This is correct because saturation means the maximum amount has dissolved at that temperature.
This is wrong because a saturated solution contains dissolved solute.
This is wrong because saturation does not require two liquids.

quiz.stem: What happens when more sugar is added after a sugar solution has become saturated?
options: It settles at the bottom.
It changes into water.
It dissolves completely in every case.
It turns the solvent into a solute.
rationales: This is correct because extra sugar will not dissolve and settles at the bottom.
This is wrong because adding sugar does not change it into water.
This is wrong because a saturated solution cannot dissolve more sugar at that temperature.
This is wrong because the added sugar does not turn the solvent into a solute.

quiz.stem: According to the section, how much sodium chloride dissolves in 100 g of water at 20°C to make a saturated solution?
options: 5 g
rationales: This is correct because the section gives 36 g of sodium chloride per 100 g of water at 20°C.
This is wrong because 100 g is the amount of water, not the dissolved sodium chloride.
This is wrong because 203.9 g is the amount of table sugar stated for 100 g of water at 20°C.
This is wrong because 5 g is used in the sugar demonstration, not the stated sodium chloride solubility.

quiz.stem: How much table sugar dissolves in 100 g of water at 20°C to form a saturated solution, according to the section?
options: 5 g
rationales: This is wrong because 36 g is the stated amount for sodium chloride.
This is wrong because 5 g is one portion used in the sugar demonstration.
This is wrong because 100 g is the amount of water in the comparison.
This is correct because the section states that 203.9 g of table sugar dissolves in 100 g of water at 20°C.

quiz.stem: What reason does the section give for table sugar having a greater solubility in water than sodium chloride at 20°C?
options: Sugar molecules are larger, so more water molecules can surround a single sugar molecule.
Sugar molecules are smaller than salt ions.
Water cannot dissolve sodium chloride.
Every solute has the same solubility in water.
rationales: This is correct because the section links larger sugar molecules with more surrounding water molecules and greater dissolution.
This is wrong because the section says sugar molecules are larger than salt ions.
This is wrong because the section states that sodium chloride does dissolve in water.
This is wrong because the section says different solutes have different solubilities.

quiz.stem: Which statement best describes how temperature affects solubility?
options: It increases greatly as temperature rises.
It does not change for any solute.
It depends on the solute; gases usually become less soluble as temperature rises.
It always decreases as temperature rises.
rationales: This is not true for all solutes; some show little change or become less soluble.
Solubility can change with temperature, so it is not always constant.
This is correct: different solutes respond differently, and gas solubility generally falls as temperature rises.
This is not true for all solutes; many solids become more soluble when heated.

quiz.stem: What is the solubility of a solute, as defined in this section?
options: The amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a particular temperature
The amount of solvent in 100 g of solute
The mass of crystals formed from any solution
The temperature at which a solute melts
rationales: This is the textbook definition of solubility.
This reverses the roles of solute and solvent and does not define solubility.
Crystals may form when a solution cools, but their mass is not the definition.
Melting point is a different property and does not define solubility.

quiz.stem: What happens to the solubility of sodium chloride in water as temperature increases?
options: The solubility of sodium chloride rises sharply.
The solubility of sodium chloride changes very little.
Sodium chloride becomes a gas.
The solubility of sodium chloride becomes zero.
rationales: The section says sodium chloride's solubility does not increase appreciably.
This matches the section's description of sodium chloride.
A change in solubility does not turn sodium chloride into a gas.
The section does not say sodium chloride becomes insoluble.

quiz.stem: Which substance is given as an example of one whose solubility in water increases with temperature?
options: Potassium nitrate
Sodium chloride
Lithium carbonate
Calcium chromate
rationales: Potassium nitrate is listed among substances whose solubility increases with temperature.
Sodium chloride's solubility does not increase appreciably with temperature.
Lithium carbonate is given as a substance whose solubility decreases with temperature.
Calcium chromate is given as a substance whose solubility decreases with temperature.

quiz.stem: Why can cooling a hot solution of a suitably soluble solid help purify that solid by crystallization?
options: Cool the solution so that crystals may form.
Heat it until all the solute becomes a gas.
Add more solvent until no solute remains.
Keep the solution hot to make crystals form.
rationales: As the solution cools, the solubility of many solids falls and crystals can form.
The section does not describe heating as changing a dissolved solid into gas.
Adding more solvent generally makes a solution more dilute rather than causing crystals to form.
Keeping the solution hot generally keeps more of such a solid dissolved.

quiz.stem: Why are soda water bottles stored in a refrigerator, according to this section?
options: They are stored in a refrigerator to keep more carbon dioxide dissolved for longer.
They are heated so the carbon dioxide dissolves more easily.
They are left open so the gas can escape.
They are frozen to remove all the dissolved gas.
rationales: The section says carbon dioxide is more soluble at low temperature, so refrigeration helps keep it dissolved.
Heating generally reduces the solubility of gases in water.
Leaving a bottle open lets carbon dioxide escape rather than keeping it dissolved.
The section recommends refrigeration, not freezing, and does not say freezing removes all gas.

quiz.stem: Which temperature effect on calcium hydroxide is stated in the section?
options: Its solubility decreases as temperature rises.
Its solubility increases sharply as temperature rises.
Its solubility is exactly the same at every temperature.
It becomes less soluble only when the solution is stirred.
rationales: The section states that calcium hydroxide becomes less soluble as temperature increases.
This is the stated trend for some other solids, not calcium hydroxide.
The section explicitly gives a temperature effect for calcium hydroxide.
Stirring is not given as the cause of the solubility change.

quiz.stem: What generally happens to the solubility of a gas in water when the water is heated?
options: The solubility of the gas decreases.
The solubility of the gas increases.
The gas changes into a solid at every temperature.
The water stops acting as a solvent.
rationales: The section states that gas solubility in water generally decreases as temperature increases.
This is the opposite of the general trend stated for gases.
The section does not say gases always become solids when heated.
Heating does not stop water from acting as a solvent.

quiz.stem: Q1.1. Matter is present in neon signs in the state of:
options: Supercritical fluid
Plasma
Gas
Liquid crystal
rationales: A neon sign does not operate with matter in a supercritical state.
Correct: the electric discharge ionizes the gas in the sign, forming plasma.
The gas is changed into plasma when the electric discharge passes through it.
A liquid crystal is not the state present in a neon sign.

quiz.stem: Q1.2. Hazardous effects of shopping bags are studied in:
options: Geochemistry
Inorganic Chemistry
Analytical Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry
rationales: Geochemistry studies chemical processes and materials of the Earth, not chiefly the environmental hazards of shopping bags.
Inorganic chemistry studies inorganic substances and their reactions.
Analytical chemistry identifies substances and measures their amounts.
Correct: environmental chemistry studies chemicals and their effects in the environment.

quiz.stem: Q1.3. The man-made polymer is:
options: Starch
Polystyrene
Protein
Cellulose
rationales: Starch is a naturally occurring polymer.
Correct: polystyrene is a synthetic, man-made polymer.
Proteins are naturally occurring polymers made by living organisms.
Cellulose is a naturally occurring polymer in plant cell walls.

quiz.stem: Q1.4. The crystals of which substance has rhombic shape?
options: Brass
Sulphur
Graphite
Bronze
rationales: Brass is an alloy, not the substance with rhombic crystals asked for here.
Correct: sulphur forms rhombic crystals.
Graphite has a layered structure rather than rhombic crystals.
Bronze is an alloy and is not the answer.

quiz.stem: Q1.5. Which liquid among the following is a colloidal solution?
options: Milk
Slaked lime used for white wash
Vinegar solution
Mixture of AgCl in water
rationales: Correct: milk is an emulsion, a type of colloid.
Slaked lime in water is not the colloidal liquid intended here.
Vinegar solution is a true solution because its particles are dissolved at molecular level.
AgCl does not form the colloidal solution intended by this question in water.

quiz.stem: Q1.6. Which of the following is a heterogeneous mixture?
options: A solution of calcium hydroxide in water
A solution of potassium nitrate in water
Hot chocolate
Concrete mixture
rationales: A solution of calcium hydroxide is treated as a solution, which is uniform in composition.
A solution of potassium nitrate is homogeneous.
Hot chocolate may appear mixed, but concrete is the clearly heterogeneous mixture in this list.
Correct: concrete has visibly different components and is not uniform throughout.

quiz.stem: Q1.7. A state of matter whose properties are between those of liquids and crystalline solids:
options: Liquid crystal
Supercritical fluid
Plasma
Dark matter
rationales: Correct: liquid crystals show properties between those of ordinary liquids and crystalline solids.
A supercritical fluid is formed above its critical temperature and pressure.
Plasma is an ionized gas.
Dark matter is not the state of matter described in the question.

quiz.stem: Q1.9. A solution of KClO₃ has a solubility of about 13.2g per 100 cm³ at 40°C. How its solubility will be affected, if you decrease the temperature?
options: The solubility will increase
The solubility will decrease
The solubility will remain the same
The solubility will first increase with temperature and then it will decrease
rationales: For this solid solute, lowering the temperature does not increase its solubility.
Correct: the solubility of KClO₃ decreases when the temperature is decreased.
The solubility of this solid changes with temperature.
This option does not describe the expected effect of decreasing the temperature.

quiz.stem: Q1.10. You are studying the rate of hydrolysis of starch under different conditions of temperature. In which branch of chemistry this topic will fall?
options: Organic Chemistry
Analytical Chemistry
Biochemistry
Physical Chemistry
rationales: Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, but the question focuses on reaction rate and temperature.
Analytical chemistry concerns identification and measurement of substances.
Biochemistry concerns chemical processes in living organisms, but the stated focus is reaction rate under different temperatures.
Correct: physical chemistry studies rates of reactions and the effects of conditions such as temperature.

modelAnswer: Allotropic forms are different forms of the same element in the same physical state.
Carbon has allotropes including diamond, graphite, and graphene.
Sulphur has rhombic, monoclinic, and plastic forms.
Coal is an impure, largely amorphous form of carbon.
Diamond is a crystalline form of pure carbon.

written.text: Q1.3. What are supercritical fluids. How are they different from ordinary liquids?
modelAnswer: A supercritical fluid exists above the critical temperature and pressure of a substance.
There is no distinct boundary between its liquid and gas phases.
It can have liquid-like density.
Unlike an ordinary liquid, it can spread and diffuse in a gas-like way.

written.text: Q1.4. Define solubility of a solute. How does the solubility of solutes change with the increase in temperature?
modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution.
The solubility of most solid solutes increases as temperature increases.
The solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases as temperature increases.

written.text: Q1.5. What types of movements are present in gaseous and liquid molecules?
modelAnswer: Gas molecules have translational, rotational, and vibrational movements.
Liquid molecules also have vibrational and rotational movements.
They can move from place to place by sliding past one another.
Their translational movement is more restricted than that of gas molecules.

written.text: Q1.6. Differentiate between the areas which are studied under inorganic and organic chemistry.
modelAnswer: Inorganic chemistry studies elements and their compounds, generally excluding most carbon compounds.
Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds.

written.text: Q1.1. Preparation of solutions leads to an important process in chemistry which enables us to purify a compound through crystallization. Describe a process in which potassium nitrate is purified by crystallizing it in water.
modelAnswer: Dissolve the impure potassium nitrate in the minimum amount of hot water to prepare a saturated solution.
Filter the hot solution to remove insoluble impurities.
Allow the clear filtrate to cool.
Potassium nitrate crystallizes as its solubility decreases on cooling.
Filter off the crystals and dry them; soluble impurities remain in the mother liquor.
